children: An industrial complex in eastern Libya designed to produce lower-carbon iron for steelmakers is expected to attract about $2.5 billion in investment, with commercial production due to start in early 2028, the chairman of the Turkish-Libyan joint venture developing the project told Reuters.

The plant, on the Mediterranean coast in the port city of Benghazi, will produce direct reduced iron (DRI), a key steelmaking input that can be made using natural gas rather than coal, resulting in lower carbon emissions than traditional steel production.
First announced in 2024, the project is one of the largest economic developments in territory controlled by military commander Khalifa Haftar.

Haftar has been de facto ruler of eastern Libya and much of its south since a civil war against the United Nations-recognised government in Tripoli in the wake of the NATO-backed uprising that toppled longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi.
Tensions between Haftar and Tripoli have eased significantly of late, and many foreign powers have strengthened ties with the Benghazi-based authorities they once regarded as renegades.
Companies from Turkey, one of the Tripoli government's main backers, have also invested heavily in eastern Libya in sectors including construction and energy.

The Benghazi plant is being developed by Tosyali Sulb Steel Industries, a joint venture between Istanbul-based steelmaker Tosyali Holding and Libya United Steel Company for Iron and Steel Industry (SULB).
About 90% of output will be exported, while the complex also plans to produce rebar and pipes for the Libyan market, Tosyali Sulb Chairman Ahmed Gadalla said in written responses to questions.
The facility is designed to produce about 8.1 million metric tons of DRI annually.

The Middle East was shaping up to be a major centre for lower-carbon iron production but some plans have been called into question by the Iran war and resulting disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Libya's long Mediterranean coastline leaves it well placed to serve both African markets and Europe, where rising operating costs and environmental compliance requirements are creating opportunities, Gadalla said.
Gas supply arrangements have been finalised for the project's first phase, which will produce about 2.7 million tons of DRI a year, he said.
A dedicated power station is also being built to provide a large share of the complex's electricity needs, he added.
